clue.text: Perplexed, raised issue about eastern dramatist

indicators.note: one thing placed about another wraps around it, so the outer word encloses the rest

blocks.note: to breed is to raise offspring, or issue
E is the abbreviation for eastern
Oscar Wilde, the Irish playwright

explanation.surface: Someone baffled after a playwright from the East brought up a thorny issue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised issue' reads as bringing up a topic, but it means produced offspring. Wilde is Oscar Wilde, the Irish playwright.
explanation.definitionFit: Bewildered is a straightforward synonym of perplexed: confused and unable to understand.

clue.text: Weaver's influence

blocks.note: first meaning: Nick ..., the weaver in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream
second meaning: the underlying cause, what is at the root of something

explanation.walkthrough: The possessive makes it read as one phrase about a weaver's sway; the 's is only a link. To be at the bottom of something is to be its cause.
explanation.definitionFit: Bottom names Shakespeare's comic weaver, and also the root cause or driving factor behind an event.

clue.text: Animal with one crossing a quarry

indicators.note: letters crossing something stretch over it from one side to the other, so they enclose it

blocks.note: W is a standard abbreviation for with
the Roman numeral for one
taken as written
a quarry is a pit dug for stone

explanation.surface: A beast with a single animal crossing an open quarry.
explanation.walkthrough: W and I go around A PIT: W(A PIT)I.
explanation.definitionFit: The wapiti is a large North American deer, also called the elk, so an example of an animal.

clue.text: Miss card game and become exasperated

blocks.note: to miss a chance is to lose it
patience is the British name for solitaire

explanation.surface: Someone who skips a hand of cards and gets fed up.
explanation.walkthrough: Patience is what Americans call solitaire, a one-player card game.
explanation.definitionFit: To lose patience is the idiom for running out of tolerance and becoming irritated.

clue.text: Go in to register

blocks.note: first meaning: to walk into a place
second meaning: to record or sign up, as with names in a list

explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as going inside in order to sign a register; the two halves are separate meanings joined by to.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb covers both stepping into a room and recording something, as you would an item in a ledger.

clue.text: Myrtle, for example, always gullible

blocks.note: ever means always, as in for ever
green means naive or inexperienced

explanation.surface: A woman called Myrtle who is perpetually easy to fool.
explanation.walkthrough: Myrtle looks like a woman's name, but here it is the shrub.
explanation.definitionFit: Myrtle is a shrub that keeps its leaves all year, an example of an evergreen plant.

clue.text: Stage favourites brought back

indicators.note: something brought back returns the way it came, so the word is read from its end

blocks.note: a teacher's pet is a favourite

explanation.surface: Popular performers return to the theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: A step is a stage in a process, one phase in a sequence.

clue.text: Complete, from beginning to end, hiding nothing

indicators.note: a thing hiding something conceals it inside itself, so one part goes within the other

blocks.note: through means from start to finish, as in reading a book through
O looks like zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A full account covering everything from start to finish with nothing concealed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From beginning to end' looks like part of the definition, but it is the wordplay's outer word, as in reading a book through.
explanation.definitionFit: Thorough means complete and detailed, leaving nothing undone.

clue.text: Characteristic of conventional type? Not half!

indicators.note: not half means only part survives, so half of the word is dropped

blocks.note: proper means correct, conventional
taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking whether a feature marks a conventional sort, answered with an emphatic yes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' is British slang for 'very much so', but here it cuts the second half off the word type.
explanation.definitionFit: A property is a characteristic or attribute, as in the chemical properties of a substance.

clue.text: Dog following kind print worker

indicators.note: following means coming behind, so the animal's piece is written second, after the word for kind

blocks.note: a type is a kind or sort
a setter is a breed of gun dog

explanation.surface: A friendly dog tailing someone who works at a printing press.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following' puts the dog after kind, so the pieces read in the reverse of the clue's order.
explanation.definitionFit: A typesetter arranges type for printing, a worker in the print trade.

clue.text: Ring after European snubbed in game

indicators.note: snubbed suggests a snub nose, shortened at the tip, so the word loses its last letter

blocks.note: a Pole is a person from Poland
O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: A ring offered after a European was coldly ignored during a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the ring at the end, behind the shortened European.
explanation.definitionFit: Polo is a team game played on horseback with long mallets.

clue.text: A film director should say what is to happen

definitions.text: A film director should say what is to happen

blocks.clueFragment: A film director should say what is to happen
blocks.note: surface reading: a film director literally announces each camera take as it is set up

blocks.clueFragment: A film director should say what is to happen
blocks.note: setter's reading: the idiom for being the one in charge who decides events

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase is literal for a director naming camera set-ups, and figurative for anyone in command.
explanation.definitionFit: To call the shots is the idiom for being in control and deciding what happens.

clue.text: Where H may be freely available

definitions.text: Where H may be freely available

blocks.clueFragment: Where H may be freely available
blocks.note: surface reading: H looks like a letter, or slang for a drug, being easy to obtain

blocks.clueFragment: Where H may be freely available
blocks.note: setter's reading: H marks the hot tap, and something freely available is ready to draw

explanation.walkthrough: H is printed on hot taps; the phrase also means readily available, as beer drawn from a barrel.
explanation.definitionFit: On tap means readily available whenever needed, and literally the hot water H labels comes from a tap.

clue.text: Complicated procedure to get millions invested in capital function

indicators.note: money invested in something is put inside it, so one part sits within another

blocks.note: Riga is the capital of Latvia
M is the abbreviation for million
a role is a function or job

explanation.surface: A fiddly business of putting millions into a capital-city event.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital is Riga, the capital of Latvia; 'function' is a part played, not an event.
explanation.definitionFit: A rigmarole is a long, tediously involved process or palaver.

clue.text: Come out with a mild exclamation of surprise

blocks.note: workers who come out go on strike
taken as written
light means mild, as in a light breeze

explanation.surface: Someone blurting out a gentle cry of astonishment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come out with' looks like the verb of speaking; 'come out' is to go on strike. Strike a light is an old British exclamation of astonishment.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a dated British interjection people say when startled or amazed.

clue.text: Uncomfortable, a guy after trouble

blocks.note: ill is harm or trouble
taken as written
to guy someone is to mock or tease them

explanation.surface: A man feels awkward after getting into trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: Guy is a verb here, meaning to make fun of. 'After' puts trouble first.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill at ease means uneasy or awkward, a synonym for uncomfortable.

clue.text: Fizzy cola - a cup drunk in Mexican resort

indicators.note: a fizzy drink bubbles and churns, so these letters are stirred up
a drunk person staggers about, so these letters lurch into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cup of fizzy cola drunk on holiday in a Mexican beach town.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'Fizzy' and 'drunk' read as describing the drink, yet each signals the letters being mixed up.
explanation.definitionFit: Acapulco is a well-known beach resort city on Mexico's Pacific coast.

clue.text: What comprises coaches on piece of track attached to rear of locomotive?

definitions.text: What comprises coaches on piece of track attached to rear of locomotive?

indicators.note: a piece of a word is just a bit of it, here its opening letter
the rear of a word is its tail end, so only the final letter is used

blocks.note: to coach is to train
the final letter of locomotive
the first letter of track

explanation.surface: A toy railway: carriages on a length of track hooked up behind an engine.
explanation.walkthrough: Coaches is a verb in the wordplay but a noun for railway carriages in the whole-clue reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A train set is a model railway: an engine pulling coaches along pieces of track.

clue.text: Freedom to act for actress leaving on the wagon? That's about right

indicators.note: leaving means departing, so the following letters are taken away
the remaining name goes about, around, the inserted letter

blocks.note: Cate Blanchett, the Australian film actress
TT is teetotal, abstaining from drink, as someone on the wagon is
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Asking whether an actress on a wagon is given free rein in her work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On the wagon' means not drinking alcohol, and crosswords write teetotal as TT; the actress loses those letters from her surname's end before the R goes in.
explanation.definitionFit: Carte blanche, French for a blank card, means complete freedom to act as one wishes.

clue.text: More would have us believe this is the perfect place

definitions.text: More would have us believe this is the perfect place

blocks.clueFragment: More would have us believe this is the perfect place
blocks.note: surface reading: more people would like us to think somewhere is ideal

blocks.clueFragment: More would have us believe this is the perfect place
blocks.note: setter's reading: Sir Thomas More wrote a 1516 book describing an ideal island society

explanation.walkthrough: The capital M is hidden by the sentence start; More is the Tudor statesman and author.
explanation.definitionFit: The word, coined by Thomas More for his imaginary island, now means any ideal society or place.

clue.text: Tries English vehicle

blocks.note: a judge hears, or tries, a case
E is the abbreviation for English

explanation.surface: Someone attempting to drive an English car.
explanation.walkthrough: Tries is the legal sense, a court trying a case.
explanation.definitionFit: A hearse is the vehicle that carries a coffin at a funeral.

clue.text: A royal has to name an Ivy League university

blocks.note: a prince is a royal
taken as written
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A member of a royal family must pick an elite American university.
explanation.definitionFit: Princeton, in New Jersey, is one of the eight elite private US universities of the Ivy League.

clue.text: Lowest point? A depth in Northern Ireland

indicators.note: in places these letters within the abbreviation that follows

blocks.note: NIR is an abbreviation for Northern Ireland
taken as written
D is the abbreviation for depth

explanation.surface: Asking whether a deep spot in Northern Ireland is the lowest anywhere.
explanation.walkthrough: Depth is abbreviated D, as in measurements; the A and D sit inside the abbreviation for Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: The nadir is the lowest point, literally the point directly beneath an observer.

clue.text: French composer posed with one close to stage

indicators.note: the close of a word is where it ends, so only its final letter is taken

blocks.note: a model sat, or posed, for a painter
one is the Roman numeral I, added on
the final letter of stage

explanation.surface: A French musician posed for a photo with someone near the theatre stage.
explanation.definitionFit: Erik Satie was a French composer, best known for his piano Gymnopédies.

clue.text: Least likely to continue

blocks.note: first meaning: as in the ... person you would expect
second meaning: to go on, endure

explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one phrase about something unlikely to survive; split at 'to' it gives two meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: Last as an adjective means least probable, and as a verb it means to endure or carry on.

clue.text: One way shopper could get you a tiny jumper?

blocks.note: surface reading: a shopper who goes one way to buy a small pullover
setter's reading: the word shopper can be written as S, then 'and', then hopper

explanation.surface: A shopper finding a way to buy a very small sweater.
explanation.walkthrough: A jumper is the British word for a sweater; here it is a small leaping creature. Break shopper as S + HOPPER and put AND between.
explanation.definitionFit: A sandhopper is a small crustacean that leaps about on beaches, so a tiny jumper.

clue.text: Swear word used during set-to at home

indicators.note: something used during a stretch of text sits within it, so the letters run across the words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of set-to, all of at, and the start of home

explanation.surface: Bad language heard during a domestic quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: A set-to is a fight or argument.
explanation.definitionFit: An oath can mean a swear word or curse, as well as a solemn promise.

clue.text: These areas, redeveloped, can bring peace of mind

indicators.note: an area that is redeveloped is rebuilt in a new layout, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Regenerating these neighbourhoods can make residents feel calmer.
explanation.definitionFit: Heartsease is an old word for tranquillity, freedom from anxiety, as well as the name of a wild pansy.
